#### Three shapes through one function — stack and heap at every step

**What is being answered.** The claim that batch is a special case of streaming — as code you can check.

`group(events, shape)` is one function. The three shapes differ in exactly one line, inside `keyFor`: batch keys on `chunkOf(e.pt)`, the other two on `winOf(e.et)`. Step 2 shows `bounded` and `stream` resolving to **the same heap object** — same keys, same members.

So what separates bounded from streaming? Only `closesAt`: bounded returns end-of-input for every window, streaming waits for the watermark. Step 4 catches that difference producing NONE for the last window — a window that is still open with nothing left to close it.

The animation steps through the code, holding each line long enough to read the STACK (call frames and their locals) and the HEAP (allocated arrays and objects) as they are AT THAT MOMENT. Expand any step to study it on its own.

For id 7, batch returns `chunkOf(280)` = 240 while both other shapes return `winOf(50)` = 0. One `if`, and the event lands 2 windows away from where it belongs. Nothing else in the program differs between the three shapes.

`bounded` and `stream` are the same object at `@0x200` — identical keys, identical members. They are not two algorithms. The difference between them is entirely in `closesAt`, which is the next step, and that is why batch and streaming are one model rather than two.

`bad` = [6, 7] — 22% of the dataset. Compare the two Grouping rows at key 240: batch holds [4,5,6,7], the windows hold [4,5]. This function can only compute that because it sees both clocks; a batch chunk, from the inside, cannot.

The loop runs out: no `watermarkAfter(i)` ever reaches 600, so `closesAt` returns NONE. Under `"bounded"` the first line would have returned 9 immediately — end of input closes everything. That is the ONLY difference between the two shapes, and it is also the source of unbounded state.
